answer.question: What did Acme Logistics say about their current workflow?
answer.answer: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan, VP RevOps, and Tom Alvarez, Director of Customer Success) described a workflow built on spreadsheets, Slack reminders and partial automation, with problems in the gaps between steps [1][2]. evidence.context: Internal build (in-house) is the main alternative; prospect's VP argues owning it long-term is the real cost and that the engineer would be overloaded. — Customer VP favours OrbitFlow on maintenance grounds; the engineer believes most of it could be built internally.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
evidence.context: An in-house build was an alternative Verity's engineers pushed for for about eighteen months before the customer ran out of arguments against it. — Build-in-house alternative; the stated reason for leaving was maintenance, which the customer argued would also apply to the platform.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: I had a depot manager tell me in July that he'd stopped keeping his own spreadsheet
evidence.context: Before OrbitFlow, a depot manager kept his own spreadsheet to track exceptions; he has since stopped. — Manual spreadsheet tracking is an alternative solution the customer used. Fiona presents its abandonment as evidence of OrbitFlow's value in depot exception handling. Comparison is implicit, not on features or price.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Everything else we could go back to doing the old way and survive.
evidence.context: Without OrbitFlow, Lumen could go back to the old manual way of working for most processes, but depot exception routing would be painful to lose. — Fiona names the status quo / manual process as the fallback. She says it is survivable for everything except depot exception routing, which she would miss most. This is a stated alternative, with the preference favouring OrbitFlow for that workflow.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Plenty of customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use us for business-owned workflows
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff say they will not replace everything and that customers often keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration, using OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows; prospect says a migrate-off-Microsoft proposal would lose to licensing. — Vendor positioning relative to existing Microsoft stack; prospect agrees migration proposal would fail on licensing.

claims.text: Unnamed vendors: DeltaWorks met an unremembered workflow vendor at Hannover Messe and had a prior vendor with transparent pricing. Fable Media spoke to two vendors that gate SSO as enterprise-only. Juniper's prior observability vendor used per-event pricing.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: I spoke to a workflow vendor there and I cannot remember which one, and it has been irritating me for two months.
evidence.context: Another unnamed workflow vendor was met at Hannover Messe in April. The customer cannot remember which one. — Unnamed competitor mentioned off-topic. No comparison or outcome stated. OrbitFlow staff did not identify the vendor and asked to hear it later.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: That is an honest answer. Most vendors say "yes, it handles that."
evidence.context: Other vendors generically claim they handle contract amendments mid-run; the customer found OrbitFlow's more explicit answer more honest. — Competitor claims compared on handling of mid-workflow state changes (contract amendments). Customer's view is that OrbitFlow's answer stood out from typical vendor responses.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: If you do that, you will be the second vendor this year who has.
evidence.context: A previous vendor provided a transparent pricing breakdown; the customer says OrbitFlow would be the second vendor that year to do so. First vendor not named. — Competitor compared on pricing transparency and professional services disclosure. Customer says the first vendor is not something they will name.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems.
evidence.context: Customer previously bought software that demonstrated well but could not reach their systems. Vendor name not given. — Previous unnamed software vendors compared on deployment architecture and connectivity to internal systems. Customer prioritises architecture over demos for this reason.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: Two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
evidence.context: Prospect has spoken to two other unnamed vendors that treat SSO as an enterprise-only feature, which contrasts with OrbitFlow's claim it is included on all plans. — Competitor comparison on security/SSO packaging; the competing vendors are not named.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: That's what happened with our observability vendor.
evidence.context: Prospect's prior observability vendor drove cost problems via per-event pricing, which the prospect cites as a reason to avoid per-event billing. — Customer mention of a past competing vendor, compared on pricing model; outcome was a bad experience ('twice').

conflicts.description: OrbitFlow's Maya Chen called Zapier the wrong comparison, but Fable Media's COO said it covers about 80% of needs and may be good enough. Oakhill says Zapier lacks approval forms.

not_covered: Final outcomes of most open evaluations (e.g., Ember, Kestrel, Acme) are not stated.
assumptions: 'Competitors' interpreted as any other vendor or alternative solution named or described in the call, including incumbent tools the customer currently uses.
No call types restricted because the question concerns all calls.
Search terms include common workflow automation competitors as examples; the reader should also capture competitors not on this list.
Competitors include incumbents, in-house builds and unnamed vendors.

grades.reason: Section [6] states Oakhill's Hazel Wren paid for Growth at 1,800/month for 30 users with only four logging in, and that a £500-600/month plan would have kept them.
The answer cites pricing concerns from many companies, including Cedar & Finch, Fable Media, Acme, Trafford Dental, Ember, DeltaWorks, Inkwell, Harbor Legal and others.

answer.question: What concerns did customers raise about pricing?
answer.answer: Across prospects, renewals, churned customers and cold calls, the most common pricing concern was per-seat licensing for occasional approvers [1]. Other recurring concerns were a Growth price above expectations or budget authority [2], hidden usage and services costs [3], value versus incumbent tools [4], and cost-justification to finance [5]. Churned and renewal customers raised paid-for-but-unused value and renewal pricing [6][7]. Some customers said base price was not the issue [8].

claims.text: Many prospects feared that occasional approvers or view-only users would need full seats, and several asked for the user split in writing. Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan), BrightPath Health (Priya Shah), DeltaWorks (Anika Bose), Ember Financial (Noah Williams, who described about 40 builders and up to 300 approvers), Inkwell Learning (Olivia Grant, 62 CSMs) and Harbor Legal (Samir Khan, Eleanor Brooks) all raised it. Greenline's Carlos Mendes said per-seat licensing for hundreds of supervisors would end the deal. OrbitFlow declined to quote a figure until the user model was defined and committed to itemised proposals.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: Please make that explicit in the proposal. I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan asked that the proposal make the user model explicit, fearing occasional approvers would need full seats later. — Per-seat licensing concern; Maya said pricing would be itemised and gave no exact number.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: What counts as a user? Because we'd have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or get a notification.
evidence.context: Customer asked what counts as a licensed user, since most people only approve or receive notifications rather than build. — Concern about per-seat cost exposure. OrbitFlow said builders and full workspace users are licensed, approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently, and declined to quote a figure until the user model is known.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: Please make that explicit in the proposal when it comes. I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer does not want occasional approvers to force full seat licences later on. — Forward-looking licensing concern. OrbitFlow committed to an itemised proposal covering builders, viewers, approvers, volume and one-time services separately.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: What is a user? We may have twenty people building and several hundred who only approve something.
evidence.context: Anika Bose asked what counts as a licensed user, because DeltaWorks may have about twenty builders and several hundred approval-only users. OrbitFlow (Jon/Maya) declined to give a number until the user model was defined, and said approval-only populations can be structured differently depending on package. — Customer question about per-user licensing model and seat count; vendor would not quote a figure yet.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: Please put that in the proposal explicitly. I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
evidence.context: Anika Bose required that the proposal explicitly state how occasional approvers are licensed, to avoid paying for a full seat for every approver in year two. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) agreed it would be explicit. — Customer cost concern about seat licensing for approvers; vendor committed to explicit treatment in proposal.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Make that split explicit in the proposal. I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer wants the licence split between builders and approval-only or view-only users made explicit in the proposal, to avoid discovering in year two that every approver needs a full seat. — Customer described about 40 builders and up to 300 approve/view users; Leo said approval-only populations can be structured differently and committed to an itemised proposal.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Three hundred is optimistic, by the way. It might be more.
evidence.context: Customer said the 300-user count is probably optimistic and could grow, which raises seat cost exposure. OrbitFlow (Leo) agreed to model 300 and 500 users to show the cost curve. — Hannah first said it might be more; Noah corrected to 'It's three hundred today', then Hannah agreed.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
evidence.context: Olivia Grant is concerned that seat licensing could be higher than expected, especially for CSMs who only receive tasks. — Seat counts were given as 3-4 builders and 62 CSMs (Darren confirmed 62). Maya Chen said the proposal would itemise the builder/recipient split and assumptions, and she would not quote a figure yet.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I won't quote a figure today because without that split any figure I give would mislead you in one direction or the other.
evidence.context: Maya Chen (OrbitFlow) gave only the list price for the Growth tier and declined to quote a total until seat assumptions were split out. — OrbitFlow's response to the pricing questions. Growth is listed at 1800 per month up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom priced.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
evidence.context: Customer warns that per-seat licensing for hundreds of occasional supervisors would end the deal. — Seat-count concern: supervisors approve or view roughly once a week and should not need full seats. Maya said approval-only populations can be structured differently depending on the package, but gave no number.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Six builders, several hundred approvers.
evidence.context: Customer stated the licensed population: six builders and several hundred approvers. — Lucy gave the builder count (her team of four plus two regional specialists). Carlos summarised the approver population. Maya asked for this shape to be explicit in writing before any proposal.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: What's a user? We'd have very few builders and a very large number of partners who approve something occasionally.
evidence.context: Samir Khan asked how users are defined, noting few builders and many occasional partner approvers, which bears on per-seat licensing cost. — Pricing-model question. Leo declined to give a number without the licence split between builders/full users and approval-only or notification-only users.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks said that if every partner needs a seat, the deal would be a very short conversation, and asked for the seat split in writing. — Customer signals that per-seat cost could end the deal. Leo agreed to surface the split before the customer takes anything internally.

claims.text: Several prospects found the Growth price (1,800/month for up to 30 users) too high. Cedar & Finch expected roughly 800-1,000/month, and Sophie Reed's spending authority is 15,000/year, so the decision goes to the COO and finance director. Fable Media's Imogen Price found it above her budget and objected to paying for 30 seats when she needs about 10. Her spending cap is a hard £20k against about £21.5k, and OrbitFlow said the package is fixed. Acme's Rachel Morgan found it above expectations after benchmarking against Zapier, and finance gets involved above 25k there. Trafford Dental's Yvonne Deeks said 1,800/month is not in her budget, wanting 200-300/month, and the opportunity ended on price.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
evidence.context: Customer said Growth tier price of 1,800 per month is hard for a team their size; they had expected roughly 800-1,000 per month. OrbitFlow acknowledged the gap. — Price objection raised right after OrbitFlow stated Growth pricing; Leo responded 'That's a real gap. I'm not going to pretend it isn't.'

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
evidence.context: Customer said the decision is above their own spending authority (15,000 per year), so the 1,800/month (21,600/year) price goes to the COO and finance director, a slower process. — Budget authority constraint raised in response to price; customer noted it is a slower conversation.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
evidence.context: Customer found the Growth package price above her budget expectation. — Initial reaction to OrbitFlow's quoted price; OrbitFlow responded that it is good value relative to what is being replaced.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
evidence.context: Customer objected to paying for thirty seats when she needs about ten; OrbitFlow said the thirty-user package is fixed. — Seat-count concern about package pricing; OrbitFlow said 'the price is the price'.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: It's a hard limit. And more to the point, if I have to take it to him, he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
evidence.context: Ben noted the annual cost is about £21.5k, and Imogen said her spending authority is capped at £20k, with the founder approving anything above that. — Budget authority constraint that makes the price a blocker; OrbitFlow asked if the limit was hard and got a 'hard limit' answer.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan found the quoted Growth price higher than expected and had benchmarked OrbitFlow mentally against Zapier; Maya Chen responded that it is a common anchor and the wrong one. — Customer pricing concern raised right after OrbitFlow stated tier pricing; Maya deferred a firm number until the user model is known.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year, so — yes, finance gets involved.
evidence.context: Finance involvement is required above twenty-five thousand a year, which affects the cost approval path. — Budget governance detail raised by the customer.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: Our practice management software costs us less than that for the whole group.
evidence.context: Customer said the OrbitFlow entry package price of £1,800/month is far above what their practice management software costs for the whole group, and objected to the price. — Raised after the vendor quoted the entry package; vendor deflected by saying the product is not practice management software, then tried to pivot to savings. Customer rejected the savings framing because the vendor did not know their size.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: The price is the real problem, by the way. Even if you'd been brilliant. Eighteen hundred a month is not a number that exists in my world.
evidence.context: Customer said the price is the real problem, even if the vendor had been brilliant; £1,800/month is not a number in their budget. — Customer's clearest statement that price, not pitch quality, is the blocker. Vendor asked if any number would work.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: For something like this? Two, three hundred a month, and I'd have to justify it.
evidence.context: Customer stated their acceptable budget is roughly two to three hundred a month for something like this, and that they would have to justify any spend. — Answer to vendor asking whether any number could work. Vendor responded 'Then we're not it', ending the opportunity on price.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: you'd still probably have got a no because of the price.
evidence.context: Customer said they would have stayed on the call longer had the vendor known something true about them, but would still likely have said no because of price. — Customer links price as the likely deciding factor regardless of pitch quality.

claims.text: Customers worried about hidden or unpredictable costs. Ember Financial's Noah Williams feared usage overages and a second-year invoice shock, and asked whether usage could be capped. Leo would not promise a cap before modelling volumes. Cedar & Finch distrusted later surprise charges. DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel wanted transparency on professional services and premium connectors. Harbor Legal reacted positively to separately quoted services. Juniper Cloud Tools worried about per-event charges and whether a fan-out counts as one run or six, and Marcus Chen asked for the pricing model in writing. Acme and BrightPath wanted no hidden scaling surprises. Halberd's Grace Okonkwo wanted the AI consumption cost stated as a number.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine. I've been through this with two other vendors and both times the second-year invoice was the problem, not the first.
evidence.context: Customer worried that usage overages could make the bill unpredictable as volumes grow, and that the second-year invoice would be the real problem. OrbitFlow (Leo) responded by offering to model expected volumes and agree the above-threshold overage mechanism in the contract before signing. — Noah raised it as a finance concern based on two prior vendor experiences; Leo answered that usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Can you cap it?
evidence.context: Customer asked whether the usage cost could be capped. OrbitFlow (Leo) declined to promise a specific cap structure before modelling volumes, saying mechanisms exist but a cap might have conditions. — Direct follow-up to the overage concern; Leo deferred a firm answer.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: But I'd like the overage modelling done in parallel rather than after, because if the economics don't work at scale I'd rather know in week two than week six.
evidence.context: Customer wants overage economics modelled in parallel with the pilot so they know early if pricing fails at scale. — Customer said nothing binding was needed before the pilot, but asked for the commercial modelling early.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
evidence.context: Customer asked whether per-workflow-run and premium-connector usage adds cost; expressed distrust of later surprise charges. — Usage-based pricing question; OrbitFlow said usage is scoped on runs and premium connectors and would model it.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
evidence.context: Martin Vogel does not expect the headline licence price to be a surprise, but wants transparency on professional services, premium connectors, and costs that only emerge after architecture review. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded by committing to separate line items with written assumptions and 'to be determined after architecture review' where unknown, rather than placeholder numbers. — Customer raised a concern about hidden costs; vendor response was a commitment to price transparency in the proposal. Vendor (T123) had earlier raised that significant SAP/on-premise work would be professional services and said she'd price it up front.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: That's the thing that goes wrong.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks and Samir Khan reacted positively to OrbitFlow saying professional services would be quoted separately with assumptions, after noting that implementation costs are usually where things go wrong. — Customer concern about hidden implementation costs appearing after discovery. Leo committed to a separate services line with its assumptions shown.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
evidence.context: Customer worried OrbitFlow pricing would charge per event, and Ava does not want to pay per event for high-volume Segment traffic; OrbitFlow advised filtering events upstream so only business-relevant events are sent. — Customer concern about event-based cost; vendor response was architectural (filter in AWS) rather than a price change.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: my question is whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping the event-handling layer in AWS.
evidence.context: Marcus asked whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping event handling in AWS. — Customer cost/value question raised after vendor quoted pricing; vendor said partly, depends on what counts as a run.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: if it's six, the composition pattern you're recommending is also the expensive pattern, and that's a conflict I'd want surfaced before we commit.
evidence.context: Customer asked whether a workflow fanning out to five subflows counts as one run or six, and said if it is six the recommended composition pattern is also the expensive pattern. — Billing-unit concern; vendor could not state billing semantics from memory and promised a written answer.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: I'd like the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, not after. If the economics don't work I'd rather know in week three.
evidence.context: Customer asked for the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends so economics can be assessed early. — Commercial request; vendor committed to week two.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan wants a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for moving to decision. — Pricing condition for decision; Maya said a perfectly valid outcome is not buying if the existing approach is cheaper.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
evidence.context: Customer's success criteria for any commercial model require no hidden scaling surprises in cost. — Stated as a condition for moving to a decision; OrbitFlow had given Growth pricing from 1800 a month for up to 30 users and said Enterprise is custom-priced.

evidence.speaker: Tobias Lund
evidence.quote: How much?
evidence.context: Customer asked how much the AI usage consumption element will cost. — Raised after the vendor said AI usage has a consumption element beyond the run allocation. Vendor (T097) replied that for about 400 incidents a month it is not material and promised a number in the renewal papers.

evidence.speaker: Grace Okonkwo
evidence.quote: Put the number in anyway.
evidence.context: Customer wanted the AI consumption cost figure stated explicitly, not just described as immaterial. — Follow-up to the consumption cost question. Customer wants a concrete number despite the vendor calling it not material.

claims.text: Prospects questioned value against cheaper or already-licensed alternatives. These were Zapier (Cedar & Finch, Fable Media about £2k vs £21k, Oakhill), Power Automate under existing Microsoft licensing (BrightPath, Greenline), an expanded Workato contract (Acme), a Gainsight comparison (Inkwell), and scripts at Ember. At Greenline, Maya said OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price, so the argument must be operational cost.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier
evidence.context: Customer said budget is the biggest risk and they might simply be over-buying, keeping Zapier instead. — Customer stated the value does not yet close the gap versus tools already paid for; OrbitFlow said it would rather they conclude that in July.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
evidence.context: Customer said they are not yet convinced the value closes the gap between OrbitFlow and tools they already pay for. — Value-for-money concern at end of call; OrbitFlow called it a fair position.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Price and complexity are the two risks. And honestly, we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough
evidence.context: Customer said Zapier, at about two thousand, is the cheaper alternative and that they may stick with Zapier plus process discipline, which the customer frames as a price and complexity risk. — Competitive price comparison; OrbitFlow argued they'd be back in eighteen months, and the customer replied they would have saved £21k in the meantime.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
evidence.context: Customer says Zapier at about £2,000-£2,500 a year is roughly a tenth of the OrbitFlow cost, and an alternative that makes the OrbitFlow price hard to defend. — Price comparison against a competitor; customer accepts Zapier loses approval steps and run history.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
evidence.context: Customer's procurement weighs heavily that Power Automate is already covered by an existing Microsoft agreement, so a new spend must justify itself against that. — Cost comparison framing. OrbitFlow agreed a full migration off Microsoft would lose on licensing; customer agreed.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
evidence.context: Customer says OrbitFlow must be materially better than the embedded Power Automate, since it is already licensed and approved, to justify switching. — Value-for-money concern tied to the incumbent's licensing; OrbitFlow (Maya) responded by asking what 'materially better' would look like, and Lucy and Carlos named troubleshooting and reusability.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
evidence.context: Customer says Power Automate's favourable licensing matters more than they would like it to. — Cost concern about the incumbent's licensing position; Maya did not dispute it.

evidence.speaker: Lucy Hart
evidence.quote: What about the Power Automate licensing thing? Because that's genuinely part of the comparison.
evidence.context: Customer raised Power Automate licensing as part of the comparison and asked how OrbitFlow compares on it. — Question about licence cost versus the incumbent; Maya replied that OrbitFlow cannot beat bundled licensing on price and that the argument must be operational cost.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan said the real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Competitive/budget objection; Maya agreed to write it as a pilot exit criterion.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: Which is why I want the model to be honest. If the answer is "expand Gainsight, it's cheaper", I want to be able to say that.
evidence.context: Customers want a cost model that compares OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight, including implementation effort on both sides, and Darren wants it to be honest even if Gainsight comes out cheaper. — Olivia links the earlier Gainsight failure to implementation effort, not licensing. Maya Chen agreed to build the comparison that way and said she would rather lose than hide a cheaper Gainsight answer.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
evidence.context: Customer noted that keeping scripts and documenting them is cheaper and will likely be proposed internally as an alternative to OrbitFlow, which is a value-for-money pressure. — Raised in the competitive discussion; Hannah agreed it would be proposed and would waste about two months. Leo answered by addressing it in pilot criteria.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: That's the argument I'd have to make internally, yes.
evidence.context: Customer says the case for switching has to rest on operational cost, not licence cost, and that making it internally is the argument they would need to make. — Carlos accepted Maya's framing that six people fielding troubleshooting tickets may outweigh the licence delta. Maya suggested measuring the time, and Carlos agreed to measure it. Lucy's day-a-week figure was a guess, as the call later confirmed.

claims.text: Customers needed an ROI or business case that finance would accept. Acme's Rachel Morgan wanted a clearer ROI story and would not frame it as headcount reduction. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed could not put 'vibes' in a spreadsheet. Harbor Legal had no cost figure for delay. Inkwell's Darren Wu doubted the attribution of renewal ROI. Pinewood's Graham Attwood said 'we'll do some training' would not convince his finance director.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan said she could justify the cost only with replacing enough manual work and possibly some Gainsight spend, and needs a clearer ROI story than time savings. — Value-for-money concern; she explicitly ties justification to a stronger ROI case.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
evidence.context: Rachel Morgan said she would not sell the case internally as headcount reduction; the stronger case is consistency and speed. — Value concern about how the ROI can be presented to finance; OrbitFlow proposed baselining pilot metrics.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I can't put "vibes" in a spreadsheet for the finance director.
evidence.context: Customer said Zapier's Growth-level pricing gap is tied to the need for a budget case; they cannot put 'vibes' in a spreadsheet for finance. — Customer explained difficulty building the cost business case for the finance director.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Do we have a number for what it costs?
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks asked whether there is a cost figure for delayed matter opening and admitted the firm has none, only time-to-open data. — Customer lacks a cost basis to justify spend. Leo responded that the client-facing cost of delay is the real number to use.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: It's also harder to evidence.
evidence.context: Samir Khan said the value of the delay cost is harder to evidence. — Follow-on to the value question; Eleanor responded that everything worth measuring is harder to evidence.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: That's the argument, and it's a good one, but it relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
evidence.context: Darren Wu challenges the ROI argument for renewal retention because the renewal impact cannot be attributed to intervention, and says finance is sceptical of customer success business cases. — Olivia's ROI case relies on intervention preventing non-renewals. Maya Chen responded by proposing a leading indicator (time from first signal to first intervention) that is measurable and attributable.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: 'we'll do some training' is not going to convince my finance director.
evidence.context: Customer says the enablement offer must be justified in financial terms because the finance director will need convincing. — Budget concern about the value of the enablement proposal. Ruth and Leo then made enablement free of charge, which answered the concern.

claims.text: Churned customers said they paid for value they did not use. Oakhill's Hazel Wren paid for Growth with 30 users when four logged in and said the roughly £19k a year was not worth it. She said a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them, and that vendor did not flag the under-use. Verity Payments said they paid a premium for business-user autonomy that did not materialise. Kwame Boateng said price was partly, but not primarily, why they chose Workato. He said they might have accepted a higher price that included paid enablement.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
evidence.context: Customer says Growth plan at £1,800/month for 30 users was paid for while only four people logged in, so they bought more than they needed. — Core pricing concern: paying for unused seats/capacity on Growth tier; customer frames it as the reason for churn.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year to a company our size.
evidence.context: Customer says the annual cost (about £19k) is hard to justify for a company their size, and that the value of the features they'd lose is not worth that price. — Value-for-money objection; customer says the three things they'd lose matter but are not worth £19k a year to a company their size.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer
evidence.context: Customer says they would have been more likely to keep buying if a smaller, cheaper plan (about £500-£600/month) existed; the entry point of Growth priced them out. — Customer's complaint about the lack of a lower-priced tier; vendor confirmed no such plan exists.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something.
evidence.context: Vendor (Ruth) says the account was not monitored for seat under-use, and customer says someone should have flagged the four users on a thirty-user plan. — Customer criticism that vendor did not raise the over-licensing; vendor acknowledged the data is looked at but rarely acted on for accounts this size.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
evidence.context: Customer said the licence cost was being justified by a business-user autonomy benefit that was not materialising, which was a reason engineering supported leaving. — Value-for-money concern raised by the engineering manager; the stated reason for leaving was value, not only connector gap.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
evidence.context: Customer said they paid a premium for a business-user platform but used it as an engineering tool, which was not worth the premium. — Value-for-money objection about the premium paid versus actual use.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: Less. Not dramatically less.
evidence.context: Customer said Workato's price is less than OrbitFlow's but not dramatically less, and that price was only partly the reason for switching. — When asked if the switch was a price decision, customer said it was partly price at the margin but not primarily price. OrbitFlow (Maya) asserted it was not a price decision and customer partially agreed.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: It's partly a price decision, because at the margin we could justify one and not the other. But no, it's not primarily price.
evidence.context: Customer said the decision was partly a price decision because at the margin they could justify one platform and not the other. — Qualification of the price factor; customer said it was not primarily price.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: 'this is eighty thousand for the platform and twenty-five for six months of someone sitting with your team', I might have said no.
evidence.context: Customer said that for a future purchase they would accept a higher platform cost if paired with a cost for a person to build workflows, suggesting pricing should include the enablement cost. — Customer's pricing suggestion for winning them back; OrbitFlow (Maya) framed it as a product and pricing point.

claims.text: Renewal customers raised several pricing concerns. Lumen Retail's Fiona Bright and Devan Shah said the run tier was wrong, disputed 20,000 runs burned in a March retry storm, and asked for seat reduction and tier increase to be shown separately. Fiona was relieved at a 7% uplift versus the 15% she feared, weighed 9% for 40% more capacity, and asked about multi-year discounts. Pinewood's Graham Attwood and Nadia Rahman said they pay for Enterprise and four builder licences while getting little value, and Graham asked about discounting a six-month term, which was not discounted. Halberd's Grace Okonkwo accepted the 7% uplift without pushback.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Were we charged for those?
evidence.context: Customer questioned whether overage charges were applied and was told two of the overages were waived; she states the run tier is wrong, pointing to a pricing/tier concern. — Customer concern about overage billing and run tier; OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded that two of four overages were waived (March retry storm, May proactive flag).

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
evidence.context: Customer said the run tier is wrong after overages, implying the current contracted volume is mis-sized and costing them. — Follow-on to overage discussion; OrbitFlow agreed the run tier is wrong and moved to propose a higher tier.

evidence.speaker: Devan Shah
evidence.quote: from our side we did nothing wrong and it cost us twenty thousand runs.
evidence.context: Customer said the March retry storm cost them twenty thousand runs they felt were not their fault, questioning whether they are being charged for vendor-side or unavoidable usage. — Customer pushed back on run consumption from an incident; OrbitFlow said configuration could help but downstream outages will still burn runs.

evidence.speaker: Devan Shah
evidence.quote: Can you show that? The two things separately?
evidence.context: Customer questioned whether the seat reduction and run tier increase are being used to inflate the total; asked for the two changes to be shown separately because a finance director will ask what changed. — Customer scrutiny of renewal pricing structure; OrbitFlow committed to itemised line items and said the seat reduction is genuine.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
evidence.context: Customer was braced for a large price increase (fifteen percent) and expressed relief when told the uplift was seven percent. — Customer expectation about renewal uplift; OrbitFlow confirmed a seven percent list uplift applying to all customers.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
evidence.context: Customer reacted to the total renewal increase, framing nine percent as a price for forty percent more capacity plus a new use case, indicating value-for-money evaluation. — Customer weighing value; OrbitFlow said total is about nine percent above this year, or about fourteen if nine seats kept.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: What about multi-year? Is there anything in it for us?
evidence.context: Customer asked about multi-year discount and whether there is anything in it for them; wanted the discount quantified before deciding. — Customer asking about term-based savings; OrbitFlow said a two-year term fixes year-two uplift and discount needs modelling.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: And the honest position — that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little — matches what I'd concluded myself, which is reassuring.
evidence.context: Customer says Pinewood is paying for Enterprise while getting very little value from it. — Graham's view, reached independently and said to be matching his own conclusion. Leo had earlier said Enterprise is probably not worth it for what they use. This is value-for-money concern about the tier.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: We've got four builder licences. One person uses it.
evidence.context: Customer questions the value of the four builder licences, since only one person uses them. — Raised while discussing why the workflows are stalled. Licence utilisation is a cost/value concern. OrbitFlow's response was to offer enablement, not to change licence count.

evidence.speaker: Nadia Rahman
evidence.quote: Audit export — no. Residency — we're UK only and we're on the EU region, so, technically yes, but it's not a requirement anyone's written down.
evidence.context: Customer says they pay for Enterprise features they don't use, such as audit export and a requirement for EU residency that was never documented. — Nadia was asked which Enterprise features they use. OrbitFlow (Leo) then offered a cheaper Growth tier, which was ruled out because it removes SSO.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: Would you discount six months?
evidence.context: Customer asks whether OrbitFlow would discount a six-month term. — Raised as a question about the shorter renewal option. Leo answered that six months is priced pro-rata at the annual rate with no short-term premium or uplift, and no discount.

evidence.speaker: Grace Okonkwo
evidence.quote: Seven percent on a number that size is not worth an hour of my life.
evidence.context: Customer accepted a seven percent standard uplift on renewal without pushing back, judging it not worth the effort to contest. — Customer raised no objection to the price increase. Vendor (T006) presented it as the only change at renewal; the customer dismissed negotiating over it.

claims.text: Several customers said the base price itself was not their concern. These were Ember Financial's Noah Williams, DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel, Harbor Legal's Eleanor Brooks, Juniper's Marcus Chen (usage economics were the open question) and Greenline's Carlos Mendes (price defensible for central operations, licensing model unclear).

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
evidence.context: Customer said the Enterprise price range was roughly what they expected for an enterprise workflow product, so base price is not their concern. — Said after Leo gave the Growth price (eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users) and said Enterprise is custom priced.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
evidence.context: Martin Vogel does not expect the headline licence price to be a surprise, but wants transparency on professional services, premium connectors, and costs that only emerge after architecture review. OrbitFlow (Maya Chen) responded by committing to separate line items with written assumptions and 'to be determined after architecture review' where unknown, rather than placeholder numbers. — Customer raised a concern about hidden costs; vendor response was a commitment to price transparency in the proposal. Vendor (T123) had earlier raised that significant SAP/on-premise work would be professional services and said she'd price it up front.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: The enterprise range itself doesn't worry me. We buy expensive software.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks said the enterprise price range does not worry her but that scope does, and she would not build a business case around privileged-content use because it would be rejected. — Customer accepts the Enterprise pricing tier but ties any business case to low-risk operational scope. OrbitFlow (Leo) agreed to scope the proposal to the low-risk tier and mark privileged content out of scope rather than as an upsell.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: The base price seems plausible.
evidence.context: Marcus said the base price seems plausible but raised the usage-limit economics as the open question. — Customer reaction to quoted base price; conditional on usage limits.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
evidence.context: Customer says the price may be defensible for central operations but needs to understand the licensing model. — Pricing response to Maya's commercials (Growth at 1,800 a month up to 30 users; Enterprise custom). Maya did not give a number, citing the need for builder versus approver counts.

answer.question: Why did customers who left decide to leave?
answer.answer: Both churned customers say the product was mismatched to how they would actually use it, though the details differ. Verity Payments says the real cause was that no one in operations built workflows, so it paid for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool [1][2][3]. Oakhill Property says it bought more than it needed and was over-licensed, and it is moving to a far cheaper Zapier setup [5][6][7]. Contributing factors included enablement and support gaps, sales-process issues, and a competitor's engineering-facing strengths [4][8][9][10].

claims.text: Verity Payments' Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations) said the connector gap was real but was not why they left; it was "the thing we pointed at." He said the real cause was that nobody in operations built workflows and that Verity never had a dedicated operations role, because he thought the product removed that need.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
evidence.context: Customer Kwame Boateng says the real reason Verity left was that nobody in operations built workflows; the connector gap was what they pointed at, not the true cause. — Stated reason differs from underlying reason; customer explicitly corrects Sarah's connector explanation

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: We never had that and I never asked for it, because I thought the product removed the need for it.
evidence.context: Verity never had a dedicated operations role to build and maintain automations; customer says the product was assumed to remove this need. — Root cause per customer; OrbitFlow staff say the product's operating model guidance states this but customer never saw it

claims.text: Verity bought OrbitFlow for business-user autonomy, but engineering built every production workflow, so Kwame said they paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. Engineering manager Sarah Lindqvist said the licence cost was being justified by autonomy that wasn't materialising, and they were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose selling point was that they wouldn't have to.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool.
evidence.context: Verity bought OrbitFlow for business-user autonomy but every production workflow was built by engineering, so they paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. — Core reason for leaving; mismatch between pitch and use

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations.
evidence.context: Engineering manager says the licence cost was being justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising, and they were maintaining custom integrations despite the platform promising they would not have to. — Engineering-side reason for leaving

claims.text: Verity chose Workato partly for a stronger core banking connector and an engineering-facing story (recipes as code, CI). Kwame said price was not the primary reason. Some of Sarah's engineers also wanted to build in-house, and she ran out of arguments against it after eighteen months. The decision became inevitable around February and was formalised in June.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: it's not primarily price.
evidence.context: Workato was chosen over OrbitFlow partly for a stronger core banking connector and stronger engineering-facing story (recipes as code, CI); customer says pricing was only partly a factor and not primary. — Competitor moved to: Workato; price a secondary factor

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
evidence.context: Engineering team was split: Sarah's engineers wanted to build in-house, and she eventually ran out of arguments against that; Workato was chosen with positive engineering-facing reasons. — Contributing factor and tipping reason for choosing Workato

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: Though I'd say the decision became inevitable in about February and it took us until June to admit it.
evidence.context: Verity had decided internally by about February and formally in June; Workato evaluation started by March and gained momentum. — Timing of decision

claims.text: Verity also cited enablement and support problems. Onboarding was two days for eight people, six of whom never used the product again, and paid sessions offered in January were declined. Kwame said that if someone had sat with two of his people for a week in the first quarter, they'd still be a customer, and that the service was never offered to them. Sarah said support was inconsistent: an April connector request got an accurate but useless answer, while Workato's SE built a custom connector in three days unbilled. She did not call this the primary reason.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: Six of them never touched it again.
evidence.context: Verity received limited enablement: a two-day onboarding for eight people, six never used it again, and no help until OrbitFlow offered paid sessions in January, which were declined. — Onboarding/adoption problem; OrbitFlow staff acknowledge hands-on service is paid add-on

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
evidence.context: Customer says hands-on build sessions would have kept them, but OrbitFlow's sitting-with-team service is a paid professional services engagement that was never offered to them. — Onboarding gap; Maya acknowledges the paid add-on may be the problem

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: That was an accurate and completely useless answer.
evidence.context: Support quality was inconsistent, and Verity felt treated as a small account; a April connector request got only a template-not-found answer, while Workato's SE built a custom connector in three days unbilled during evaluation. — Contributing factor to leaving; not the primary reason per Sarah

claims.text: Oakhill Property's Hazel Wren (Operations Director) said the whole answer was that they bought something they didn't need. They were on Growth at £1,800/month for 30 users, and only four people ever logged in.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: Right. We bought something we didn't need. That's the whole answer.
evidence.context: Customer says the core reason for leaving is that they bought a product they did not need; the purchase was oversized for a small team's automation needs. — Decision maker's primary explanation; customer states no product complaint.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
evidence.context: Customer was on Growth at £1,800/month for 30 users while only four people ever logged in. — Over-licensing relative to actual usage was the driver of the cost problem.

claims.text: Hazel said the workflows worked perfectly and she has no product complaint. She also said the last year's service was fine.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: They worked perfectly. That's the frustrating part. I've got no complaint about the product at all.
evidence.context: Customer says the workflows worked perfectly and she has no product complaint. — Explicitly rules out product quality as the reason for leaving.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: Fine. Genuinely fine.
evidence.context: Customer says OrbitFlow's last-year service was fine and support tickets were answered; OrbitFlow contact was only a product announcement email. — Support not a reason for leaving; vendor outreach was thin.

claims.text: Oakhill is moving to Zapier at about £2,000–2,500 a year, roughly a tenth of the OrbitFlow cost. Hazel accepts losing approval steps and run history, which she will miss, and Zapier can't do contractor sign-off approval forms.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
evidence.context: Customer is moving to Zapier at roughly £2,000–2,500 a year, about a tenth of the OrbitFlow cost. — Named competitor/replacement; cost is the main driver.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We'll lose the approval steps and we'll lose the run history, which I'll genuinely miss.
evidence.context: Customer acknowledges Zapier will lack approval steps and run history, and that Zapier cannot do contractor sign-off approval forms, which is a capability gap. — Hedge: capability loss accepted as worth less than the cost difference.

claims.text: Hazel said the original sale promised a scaling roadmap (compliance, service charges, contractor management) that never happened because the team lacked capacity. She said they paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty. Account Executive Alastair McCrae acknowledged he should have pushed harder on whether they had capacity for the roadmap.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty.
evidence.context: Customer says the original sale promised a scaling roadmap (compliance, service charges, contractor management) that never happened because the team lacked capacity; the purchase was priced against a future that did not occur. — Contributing factor: over-purchase based on sales-process roadmap; both sides were enthusiastic.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about.
evidence.context: Alastair McCrae acknowledges he should have pressed on whether the customer had capacity for the roadmap sold. — Vendor admission about the sales process.

claims.text: Oakhill's value also faded over time: the pain the product solved stopped feeling urgent, and the invoice was questioned at renewal. Hazel said OrbitFlow should have flagged the unused seats and that a plan at £500–600/month would have kept her. OrbitFlow's Ruth Adeyemi confirmed there is no plan smaller than Growth and that the account was in a segment with no assigned CSM. Hazel would consider a smaller plan only if it included approval forms.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: Nobody remembers how bad it was.
evidence.context: Customer says the value faded over time: the pain the product solved stopped feeling urgent, and at renewal the invoice was questioned. — Contributing factor: value became invisible at renewal rather than a product failure.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer
evidence.context: Customer says OrbitFlow should have flagged the unused seats after six months and that no smaller plan existed, which would have kept her as a customer. — Contributing factor: lack of proactive account monitoring and no entry tier below Growth.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff confirm there is no smaller plan than Growth and that the account was in a segment without an assigned CSM, so under-usage was not caught. — Vendor response explaining the lack of intervention.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do and it's the only thing I'll actually miss.
evidence.context: Customer would only consider a smaller plan if it included approval forms; without them she would not buy. — Hypothetical retention condition.

claims.text: Kwame said Verity's sales process sold to their enthusiasm rather than their capability, and that nobody asked who would build workflows. He said Verity was probably the wrong customer, or was sold the product for the wrong reason.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: You sold to my enthusiasm rather than to my capability.
evidence.context: Customer says the sales process sold to their enthusiasm rather than their capability; nobody asked who would build workflows. — Sales-process criticism acknowledged by Maya

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: I think we were the wrong customer for the product, or the product was sold to us for the wrong reason.
evidence.context: Customer says Verity was probably the wrong customer for the product, or was sold the product for the wrong reason. — Hedged overall view

claims.text: Verity's trigger in February was that the settlement reconciliation workflow couldn't be built economically. The settlement provider had no OrbitFlow connector, and custom integration effort exceeded the value.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them.
evidence.context: Settlement reconciliation workflow could not be built economically because the settlement provider had no OrbitFlow connector and custom integration effort exceeded value. — Specific product gap raised as the February trigger; customer notes Workato also lacks the connector

conflicts.description: Sarah raised the missing settlement-provider connector as the February trigger, while Kwame said the connector gap was only what they pointed at and not the real reason, which was that nobody in operations built workflows.

answer.question: Has anyone from the vendor given inconsistent answers about the product?
answer.answer: Yes. The strongest cases are Alastair McCrae on Fable Media (overclaims later hedged) and Trafford Dental, Maya Chen on pricing and contract terms, Ruth Adeyemi on churn and at-risk calls, and Nina Patel on AI controls [1][2][3][4][5][6]. Some inconsistencies are directly stated, and others are inferred or only appear alongside other statements [7].

claims.text: Alastair McCrae (Fable Media) made several confident claims that he then hedged or changed. He said SSO is included on all plans, then was only 'fairly sure'. He said monthly billing is 'usually fine', then needed to check with his manager. He said the thirty-user minimum is the package, then said the price covers the platform rather than seats. He said alerting is event-driven, then that two workflows may be needed. He called Zapier 'a toy', then softened. He said a referenced customer renewed, then said he wasn't sure. He also said the product is 'fully GDPR compliant' and 'completely no-code'.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, so SSO's included on all our plans, that's standard.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said SSO is included on all plans. — Security/plan claim; later the vendor said he was only 'fairly sure' and would confirm, and customer noted competitors treat it as enterprise-only.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, monthly's usually fine, we can sort something out.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff first said monthly billing is 'usually fine' and that he could not see a problem, then said he needed to check with his manager; later he was asked to confirm and said he would check. — Pricing term hedged and unconfirmed; the vendor did not confirm monthly billing on the call.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: The thirty is the package, so the price is the price.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the thirty-user minimum is part of the package and seats cannot be reduced to ten, then said the price covers the platform rather than seats. — Seat-count pricing claim; the vendor changed framing from fixed package to platform pricing.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: It'd be event driven, so when the record changes it fires.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff described the event-driven alerting as firing on record change, then said a scheduled workflow could cover dates passing, but said two workflows was 'possibly' needed and unconfirmed. — Hedged/changed answer on how date-slip alerts work.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, all of that's doable.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the requested HubSpot-to-Asana-to-Slack workflow with date-slip alerting is doable, but admitted the demo environment could not show it and the scheduled alert approach needed an SE check. — Capability claim that was later qualified: alerting on date slips may need two workflows, and architecture unconfirmed.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Exactly. That's exactly it. Zapier's a toy, basically, once you get past —
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff claimed the competitor-style comparison that Zapier is 'a toy' at scale, then accepted the customer's view that Zapier does about eighty percent of what they need. — Vendor disparaged Zapier; customer pushed back and the vendor softened to 'at scale'.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: I moved off that account so I'm not across the detail. But they renewed, I think.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff gave a customer reference story and said a referenced customer renewed, then said he was not sure and would check. — Unverified claim about a past customer outcome; vendor said he moved off the account.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: And we're fully GDPR compliant, so that's all covered.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the platform is fully GDPR compliant. — Compliance claim made in response to customer security questions.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: That's fine, it's completely no-code.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the product is 'completely no-code' and that the workflow setup needs no code for the customer's use case. — Usability claim; customer said they have no IT team and an ops manager would administer it.

claims.text: Alastair McCrae (Trafford Dental) said OrbitFlow can integrate with anything that has an API, then said 'I'd have to check' whether the NHS e-Referral system has one.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: We can integrate with anything that's got an API, so —
evidence.context: Vendor claims OrbitFlow can integrate with anything that has an API. — Alastair responding to customer's question about NHS e-Referral integration; a general capability claim about connectors, not verified for this system.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: I'd have to check.
evidence.context: Vendor could not confirm whether the NHS e-Referral system has an API, undercutting the earlier blanket integration claim. — Hedge/retraction within the same call: after claiming integration with anything with an API, vendor said he would have to check whether the customer's referral system has one.

claims.text: Ruth Adeyemi (Oakhill Property) said 'There isn't one' regarding a smaller plan than Growth, then asked whether the customer would buy a $500/month five-workflow plan. Alastair McCrae confirmed he had told the customer no smaller plan existed. Ruth also said producing screenshots is not a service offered while offering to arrange it.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: There isn't one.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said there is no smaller plan than Growth; the entry point is Growth. — Customer said she was told the entry point is Growth. Ruth's flat denial is later undercut by her own hypothetical about a five-hundred-a-month plan in T126.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi

claims.text: Nina Patel (Ember Financial) said AI steps are explicit and enterprise customers can disable AI. Ruth (Pinewood) said a workflow has been failing 'every four hours since January', which a finding infers does not match her later 'two thousand times' figure. Jon Bell (Acme Logistics) hedged some claims after giving them, and Maya Chen also hedged her non-training assurance by moving it to the contract.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps inside a workflow. They're not ambient and they're not in the execution path unless you put them there. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely.
evidence.context: AI steps are explicit and not in the execution path unless the customer puts them there; administrators can restrict models and enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. — Governance answer to Hannah's model-risk gate. Later, T038 says the rule that AI output cannot feed decisions is only a design convention, which is a narrower control than this framing suggests.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. I'm not going to tell you there's a switch labelled "AI outputs cannot feed decisions", because there isn't.
evidence.context: AI outputs cannot be enforced as leaf nodes by the platform; it is a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. — Direct correction of the design principle Nina proposed at T036. It sits alongside her T026 claim about controls, and Hannah asked for it to be recorded as a known limitation (T201).

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: It's been failing since January. Every four hours.
evidence.context: The 'TEMP - do not use' workflow has been failing since January, every four hours. — Vendor's account of the failure cadence. Inferred inconsistency in the vendor's figures.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Noted, and agreed — that belongs in the contract, not on a call.
evidence.context: Non-training of customer data was to be documented in the contract rather than asserted on the call. — Vendor AE hedged the earlier verbal assurance by moving it to contract.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: If your policy is strict, AI can be disabled, or we scope the pilot to deterministic steps while security reviews model usage separately.
evidence.context: Vendor said AI is optional steps and may be disabled, and said model vs. rules is per use case; later said AI could be scoped out of pilot pending security review. — Vendor scoping hedge on AI, offered as alternative to block security review.

answer.question: Which cold calls produced a follow-up, and what did the successful ones have in common?
answer.answer: Four of the five cold calls ended with some follow-up agreed, but only Beacon Housing Trust produced a firm, dated meeting [1]. Silverline Travel and Kestrel Robotics agreed to a short written note with a meeting conditional on its quality [2][3]. Quarry Ridge Foods agreed only to one email [4], and Trafford Dental Group effectively rejected OrbitFlow [5]. The calls that went furthest shared a problem-specific pitch and a no-demo, discovery-style ask [6].

Maya Chen was to check framework coverage and send technical requirements, and Ade would send the frameworks. If the vendor is on none of the frameworks, Maya said she would tell him and they would decide whether to continue.

grades.reason: Answer says the connector gap was only what they pointed at and the real reason was different; evidence quotes 'The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left.'

answer.question: What did Verity Payments say was the reason they left?
answer.answer: Verity's Head of Operations, Kwame Boateng, said the connector gap was only what they pointed at; the real reason was failed business-user adoption, so the platform was used as an engineering tool and wasn't worth the premium [1]. Engineering Manager Sarah Lindqvist added reasons: maintaining custom integrations and internal pressure to build in-house [2]. Price was not primary [3], and support was a contributing feeling but not the reason [4]. They moved to Workato [5].

claims.text: Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations) said the connector gap was real but not why they left; it was "the thing we pointed at." The real reason was that nobody in operations built anything, so they paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool, which was not worth the premium.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
evidence.context: Customer said the connector gap was real but was not why they left; the real reason was that nobody in operations ever built anything, so the platform was used as an engineering tool and was not worth the premium. — Kwame pushes back on Sarah's framing that the connector gap was the reason; he identifies the real reason as failed business-user adoption. Stated reason vs. real reason is contrasted.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
evidence.context: Customer said they paid a premium for a business-user platform but used it as an engineering tool, which was not worth the premium. — Kwame's summary of the failed adoption; the premium is the licence cost.

claims.text: Kwame said they never had a dedicated operations automation role because he thought the product removed the need for one, which is the root cause of the failed adoption.

evidence.speaker: Kwame Boateng
evidence.quote: We never had that and I never asked for it, because I thought the product removed the need for it.
evidence.context: Customer said the team never had a dedicated operations automation role, and the product was expected to remove the need for one. — Root cause of failed adoption per customer; vendor acknowledged the product changes rather than removes the need for the role.

claims.text: Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager) said they left because they were maintaining custom integrations on a platform whose selling point was avoiding that, and the licence cost was justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising. Two of her engineers also wanted to build in-house, and after eighteen months of arguing against them she ran out of arguments.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations.
evidence.context: Engineering manager said they left because they were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose selling point was avoiding that, and the licence cost was justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising. — Sarah's engineering-side reasons for supporting the exit; she also says her team liked the run history and exception queues.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: And because two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.

evidence.context: Customer said price was not the primary reason; it was partly price at the margin. — Vendor asked whether it was a price decision; customer partly conceded.

answer.question: What are the most common reasons prospects hesitate to buy?
answer.answer: Across all 10 prospect calls, the most recurring hesitations were pricing and seat licensing [1], security, compliance and AI-data concerns [2], competing alternatives or build-in-house [3], and internal approval or veto gates [4]. Timing constraints [5], integration and architecture doubts [6], and ROI or proof of value [7] also recurred.

claims.text: Price and per-seat licensing fears came up in many calls. Prospects worried that occasional approvers would need full seats: Acme (Rachel Morgan), BrightPath (Priya Shah), DeltaWorks (Anika Bose), Ember (Noah Williams), Greenline (Carlos Mendes, who said it would end the evaluation), and Harbor Legal (Eleanor Brooks). Sticker shock was also stated: Acme ("more than I expected"), Cedar & Finch ($1,800/month vs. an expected $800-1,000) and Fable Media (£1,800/month, and 20 unneeded seats). Others worried about hidden or usage-based costs: DeltaWorks (professional services and premium connectors), Ember (year-two overages), and Juniper (per-event or subflow billing).

evidence.context: Price feels higher than expected; the prospect had anchored on Zapier pricing. — Price objection at the first mention of cost, before any ROI discussion. Rachel acknowledges the Zapier comparison is unfair.

claims.text: Security, compliance and AI/data handling were frequent gates. BrightPath needs a written BAA position; Ember cited model risk and auditability, with LLMs in a decision path in scope of a nine-month process. Harbor Legal raised write-path, run-log exposure, ethical-wall and retention constraints. UK residency was raised at Harbor Legal and Greenline, EU residency at Cedar & Finch and Juniper, and FERPA data boundaries at Inkwell. Several prospects wanted AI disabled or out of phase one (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal), and BrightPath, Fable and DeltaWorks wanted no-training commitments in writing or in the contract.

evidence.quote: If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.

evidence.context: Prospect will not accept a verbal assurance on the BAA; requires a written position. — Security objection handled by OrbitFlow committing to a written answer from legal and compliance.
